Queasiness is the noun that describes an uncomfortable, uneasy, unsettled feeling — most often felt in the stomach — that makes you feel like you might vomit, even if you actually don't end up vomiting. It is the state or condition of feeling queasy.

Think of it this way: queasiness is that horrible, "something is wrong in my stomach" feeling you get right before you feel truly sick. It sits in that unpleasant middle zone — you don't feel fine, but you haven't been fully sick either. It is a kind of threatening discomfort, like your body is sending you a warning signal.
The Two Main Senses of the Word

Queasiness works in two important ways — one physical, one emotional/moral. Both are equally correct and widely used.

1. Physical Queasiness (The Body)

This is the most common and straightforward meaning. It refers to a sensation of nausea — a churning, turning, unsettled feeling in the stomach that makes you feel like you are on the verge of vomiting.

Key qualities of physical queasiness:

  • It is a building or lingering feeling, not a sudden sharp pain.
  • It often comes in waves — it rises, eases a little, and rises again.
  • It can be mild (a slight stomach upset) or severe (you feel genuinely on the edge of being sick).
  • You feel uncomfortable, restless, and unable to focus on anything else.

What commonly causes physical queasiness:

  • Travelling in a car, boat, plane, or train (motion sickness)
  • Eating something that doesn't agree with you
  • An empty or overly full stomach
  • A strong or unpleasant smell
  • Anxiety or nervousness (your stomach reacts to your emotions)
  • An illness like a stomach virus or food poisoning
  • Certain medicines
  • Pregnancy (morning sickness is a well-known cause of queasiness)
  • Seeing something disturbing or disgusting

Examples:

  • The queasiness hit her the moment the boat began to rock.
  • He felt a wave of queasiness after eating the leftover fish.
  • The queasiness in her stomach made it impossible to eat breakfast before the exam.

2. Emotional or Moral Queasiness (The Mind and Conscience)

This is the figurative, but equally important, meaning of the word. Here, queasiness moves away from the body and describes a feeling of unease, discomfort, or mild disgust about something happening in the world around you — particularly something that feels morally wrong, ethically uncomfortable, or deeply unsettling to your conscience.

In this sense, queasiness is not about your stomach at all. It is about a feeling that something is not right, and you are troubled by it — even if you cannot fully explain why.

Key qualities of emotional queasiness:

  • It is a feeling of inner discomfort, unease, or moral hesitation.
  • It often arises when you witness or think about something you find wrong, unfair, or disturbing.
  • It is milder than outrage or disgust — it is more of a nagging, unsettled feeling than a strong reaction.
  • It can also describe reluctance or hesitation before doing something that makes you uncomfortable.

What commonly causes emotional queasiness:

  • Witnessing something cruel, dishonest, or morally questionable
  • Being asked to do something that goes against your values
  • Thinking about a topic that deeply unsettles you (violence, injustice, etc.)
  • Seeing a situation that feels deeply unfair but that you feel powerless about

Examples:

  • There was a queasiness among the staff when they learned how the company had been treating its workers.
  • He felt a queasiness about the whole plan — it was legal, but something about it felt deeply wrong.
  • The documentary left viewers with a queasiness that stayed with them long after it ended.

It helps to understand where queasiness sits on a scale, because it is not the most extreme word for discomfort — it describes a moderate, building, or lingering unpleasantness.

Physical scale:
Slight discomfort → Queasiness → Nausea → Vomiting

Emotional scale:
Slight unease → Queasiness → Discomfort → Disgust → Outrage

This means queasiness is serious enough to notice and be bothered by, but it has not yet reached its worst possible point.

Since you want a complete understanding, here are the related forms of this word:

  • Queasy (adjective) — the describing word. "She felt queasy on the boat."
  • Queasiness (noun) — the state or condition itself. "The queasiness wouldn't go away."
  • Queasily (adverb) — in a queasy manner. "He smiled queasily and pushed his plate away."
How Queasiness Differs from Similar Words

Many words are close to queasiness, but they are not identical.

  • Nausea — Very similar to queasiness but slightly stronger and more clinical. Nausea feels more severe and more certain to result in vomiting. Queasiness is often a milder, more unsettled version of nausea.
  • Sickness — More general and can refer to any illness. Queasiness is specifically about that stomach-turning, uneasy feeling.
  • Dizziness — Dizziness is about feeling like the world is spinning or losing your balance. Queasiness is about your stomach, not your head — though both can happen at the same time (like in motion sickness).
  • Unease / Uneasiness — Very close to the emotional meaning of queasiness, but uneasiness is more broadly about anxiety or worry. Queasiness has a slightly stronger, more visceral (gut-level) quality to it — it carries the echo of that stomach feeling even in its emotional sense.
  • Discomfort — A more general, neutral word for any unpleasant feeling. Queasiness is more specific and more vivid.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Queasiness = that "ugh, something feels wrong" feeling in your body OR your conscience, that sits uncomfortably and won't let you rest.

Whether your stomach is turning on a rocky boat, or your conscience is turning because you've seen something morally troubling — that unsettled, nagging, can't-quite-shake-it discomfort is queasiness.
